title: Caitlin Clark Suspended After 8th Technical Foul of Season
text:
Caitlin Clark Is Nearing A WNBA Suspension, But The Officials May Be Part Of The Problem

Caitlin Clark will sit out Tuesday’s game against the New York Liberty after picking up her eighth technical foul of the season Saturday in Chicago, making her the first player ever suspended under the WNBA’s technical foul accumulation rule.

The call itself is the part people are going to argue about all weekend. Late in the game against the Sky, Clark was bumped out of bounds while making a pass along the baseline and ran into a referee. She looked at the official, then turned away. The technical came at that moment, for what the official judged to be extra contact. Fever head coach Stephanie White was furious enough about it to pick up a technical of her own.

Under WNBA rules, an eighth technical in the regular season triggers an automatic one-game suspension without pay along with a $1,500 fine, and every two technicals after that carries another suspension. So the tenth would cost her another game, then the twelfth, and so on. Indiana can appeal, and if the league rescinds the technical she plays Tuesday. That is a real if. The Fever have appealed at least two of Caitlin Clark’s technicals this season and the league denied both.

The most recent denial came in July, after her seventh. That one came during a 123-88 blowout of the Connecticut Sun, when Saniya Rivers told Clark she was locking her up and Clark pointed at the scoreboard, which read 95-67 at the time. Both players got technicals. Plenty of people around the league thought it was nowhere near technical foul territory, since trash talk in a 35 point game is ordinary. The WNBA disagreed and let it stand.

What makes this history is that nobody has ever actually hit the number before. Caitlin Clark flirted with it as a rookie in 2024 under the old seven technical threshold and finished with six. She had two all of last season in a year interrupted by injuries. The league raised the limit to eight for this season, and she is the first person to reach it. Her eight are the most in the WNBA this year, and only five players have more than four.

She saw it coming and said so. After the seventh, asked whether she would dial anything back, her answer was direct. “I’m never going to back down,” she said. “I think just try to continue to control your emotions the best you can. That intensity and that fire is what makes me, me. But also knowing my team needs me, and finding a good balance of that. But I don’t think I’m going to be playing with that in the back of my head.” Weeks earlier, after a technical she called ridiculous, she joked that everyone should just pick a game on the calendar for her suspension now.

The Fever won Saturday anyway, 90-86, and the timing could be worse. Indiana is holding position at the top of the Eastern Conference and can survive one night without her, particularly with Kelsey Mitchell and Aliyah Boston playing the way they have been. The longer term math is uglier. With the tenth technical sitting out there as another automatic suspension and a stretch of the season still to play, this can stop being a one game story fast.

Saturday was chaotic well before the technical. In the first quarter, Sky guard DiJonai Carrington was ejected after a hard foul on Sophie Cunningham was upgraded to a flagrant 2 on review, with officials citing windup, impact and follow through. Cunningham was going up for a fast break layup when Carrington caught her in the head and neck area and knocked her to the floor. The bucket counted, Cunningham hit the free throw, and she had to be held back from Carrington by teammates. Minutes later, Carrington posted “WHITE PRIVILEGE” on Threads and tagged the Fever. She has not explained what she meant, and it is not clear whether she was referring to Cunningham, the officiating, or the organization.

That happened against a backdrop that has been building for weeks. Cunningham has been at the center of an ongoing WNBA fight over transgender athletes in women’s sports since comments she made in an ESPN profile. Rallies have shown up outside Fever road games. A Storm minority owner was fined and suspended for five home games after confronting demonstrators courtside in Seattle. Commissioner Cathy Engelbert sent a memo to players and teams this week about how the league is handling it. The Fever have distanced themselves from the rallies and issued statements focused on inclusion.

So the suspension is real, the rule is the rule, and Clark hit the number honestly. But anyone arguing that the officiating around the Fever has been steady this season is going to have a hard time using Saturday as their evidence.

Indiana has not said publicly whether it is appealing. Given the stakes and the way the call looked, it would be a surprise if it does not.
